qs.s: How do you smell a substance safely in the laboratory?
o: Put your nose over the container and breathe in.
Wave a little of the vapour towards your nose with your hand.
Ask the person next to you to smell it first.
Taste a tiny drop instead of smelling it.
qs.f: Rule 8, page 8: waft, never sniff. Only a little vapour should reach your nose.

qs.s: You break a test tube. What should you do?
o: Pick up the pieces by hand and put them in the dustbin.
Tell your teacher at once and sweep the glass into the broken-glass bin.
Leave it for the next class to clear.
Rinse the pieces and put them back in the rack.
qs.f: Rule 10, page 8: report everything; sweep broken glass into the broken-glass bin, never pick it up by hand.

qs.s: Which rule is broken? A pupil leaves the room without asking and goes into the prep room to fetch more chemicals. Rule broken: [a]. A pupil eats a sandwich from his bag during the practical. Rule broken: [b]. A pupil walks in with her backpack on, turns, and knocks a beaker off the bench. Rule broken: [c].
qs.f: Match each story to one of the 12 rules on page 8. These are scenarios 1, 4 and 6 on pages 9 to 10.

qs.s: Match the accident to what you do first.
p: Rinse it at the eyewash station with running water
Rinse with plenty of cold water
qs.f: "If there is an accident", page 8. In every case, tell your teacher straight away.

qs.s: Three pupils must find out which of two unlabelled liquids is vinegar. Pupil A: put your nose over the bottle and take a deep sniff. Pupil B: taste a tiny drop on your finger. Pupil C: never smell or taste an unknown liquid; ask the teacher, or waft carefully if the teacher says you may. Who is right?
qs.f: Who is right?, page 9. Never taste anything in the lab, and waft instead of sniffing.

qs.s: Why do you point a test tube you are heating away from yourself and everyone else?
o: A liquid can suddenly boil and shoot out.
The flame is easier to see.
The test tube heats up faster.
qs.f: Rule 9 and "Heating a test tube", page 8: a liquid can suddenly boil and shoot out.

qs.s: Match each hazard symbol name to what it warns you about.
p: A substance that can easily ignite and cause fires.
Causes explosion if exposed to heat, shock or friction.
A substance that has the potential to cause severe harm to living tissue and corrode metals.
Causes irritation to eyes, skin or respiratory system.
A substance that can cause harm to the environment, especially aquatic ecosystems.
x: A gas squeezed into a cylinder. It can burst if heated or dropped.
qs.f: Learn these five word for word from the Learn box on page 12.

qs.s: What does a GHS hazard pictogram look like?
o: A black symbol on white inside a red diamond.
A black symbol inside an orange square.
A red symbol inside a black circle.
A white symbol inside a yellow triangle.
qs.f: Page 12: a black symbol on white inside a red diamond.

qs.s: Which symbol warns about the more dangerous substance?
o: The exclamation mark, because it means "be careful".
qs.f: Common mistake, page 13: the exclamation mark means irritant (harmful). Skull and crossbones (toxic) is far more dangerous.

qs.s: A bottle shows a flame in a red diamond. What does it warn you about?
o: A substance that can easily ignite and cause fires.
A substance that gives off oxygen.
A gas squeezed into a cylinder.
A substance that harms water life.
qs.f: The flame symbol means flammable, page 12. Keep it away from flames.

qs.s: We use a [a] to measure the volume of a liquid. We use [b] to measure mass, in [c]. We use a [d] to transfer a few drops of liquid.
qs.f: Apparatus cards, pages 15 to 16. A balance measures mass in grams, never weight.

qs.s: A pupil must measure exactly 25 cm³ of acid as accurately as possible. Which apparatus should she use?
qs.f: Page 15: a volumetric pipette measures one exact volume, e.g. 25 cm³, very accurately.

qs.s: Which apparatus do you use to transfer small amounts of a solid?
qs.f: Apparatus cards, page 16: a spatula transfers small amounts of a solid.

qs.s: Match the apparatus to what it measures.
qs.f: Apparatus cards, pages 15 to 16.

qs.s: How many cm³ are there in 35 mL? Type the number only.
qs.f: 1 mL = 1 cm³ (page 19), so 35 mL = 35 cm³.

qs.s: Where do you read a measuring cylinder, and where must your eye be?
o: The top of the meniscus, looking down from above.
The bottom of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.
The top of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.
The bottom of the meniscus, looking up from below.
qs.f: Page 20: read the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with it.

qs.s: A measuring cylinder is numbered 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 mL. There are 5 small spaces between one number and the next. The bottom of the meniscus is 4 small spaces above the 20 mark. What is the reading in mL? Type the number only.
qs.f: Scale step = (30 − 20) ÷ 5 = 2 mL. Reading = 20 + 4 × 2 = 28 mL. Method and Worked example 1.2, page 20.

qs.s: A pupil counts the lines between 20 and 30 and gets 4 lines. There are [a] spaces between 20 and 30, so the scale step is 10 ÷ [b] = [c] mL.
qs.f: Count the spaces, not the lines (page 20). Four lines make five spaces, so the step is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 mL.

qs.s: A conical flask of acid stands on an electronic balance. Marble chips are added and the mixture fizzes. The mass is 152.6 g before the reaction and 151.2 g after it. What is the change in mass?
qs.f: Change in mass = 152.6 − 151.2 = 1.4 g. A gas was produced and escaped (Worked example 1.3, page 22).

qs.s: A measuring cylinder holds 45 cm³ of water. A stone is lowered in and the reading becomes 61 cm³. Calculate the volume of the stone in cm³. Type the number only.
qs.f: Volume of object = final volume − initial volume = 61 − 45 = 16 cm³ (page 23).

qs.s: You find the volume of a stone by displacement: you lower it into water in a measuring cylinder. Why must the stone be completely under the water?
o: So that it does not float.
Only the part under the water pushes water aside, so the rise would be too small.
So that the cylinder does not crack.
So that you can read the meniscus more easily.
qs.f: Explain, page 23: only the part of the object under the water pushes water aside.

qs.s: A stone is lowered into water in a measuring cylinder. You read the water level before (initial reading) and after (final reading). The volume of the stone is:
o: the final reading minus the initial reading
the final reading plus the initial reading
qs.f: Exam eye, page 23: the volume of the object is the difference, not the final reading.

qs.s: 1. Pour water into a measuring cylinder. Read the [a] volume. 2. [b] the cylinder and let the object slide gently down the side, so no water [c]. 3. The object must be completely under the water. Read the [d] volume.
qs.f: The steps on page 22. Slide the object in gently so that no water splashes out.

qs.s: One marble has a volume of 6 cm³. Four identical marbles are put into a measuring cylinder that holds 50 cm³ of water. What is the new reading in cm³? Type the number only.
qs.f: Volume of 4 marbles = 4 × 6 = 24 cm³; new reading = 50 + 24 = 74 cm³. Compare Practice question 8, page 31.

qs.s: Match each part of the Bunsen burner to its job.
p: heavy, so the burner does not tip over
carries gas from the gas tap to the burner
a ring you turn to open or close the air hole
the tube where gas and air mix before they burn at the top
qs.f: The parts and their jobs are on page 25.

qs.s: Safety flame: a [a] flame. The air hole is [b]. Heating flame: a [c] flame. The air hole is [d].
qs.f: Learn box, page 25: safety flame yellow, air hole closed; heating flame blue, air hole open.

qs.s: Which flame should be burning while you wait to start heating?
o: The blue heating flame, because it is hotter.
The yellow safety flame, because it is easy to see.
A blue flame with the collar half open.
Either flame, it does not matter.
qs.f: Table, page 26: use the safety flame when you light the burner and whenever you are not heating.

qs.s: A pupil lights a Bunsen burner and opens the air hole straight away. While he waits he leaves the burner on and turns to chat. What should he do instead?
o: Close the air hole so the yellow safety flame burns, and stay with the burner.
Open the air hole further so the flame is easier to see.
Move the burner to the edge of the bench.
Blow the flame out and light it again later.
qs.f: "Spot the unsafe action", page 27: close the air hole for the safety flame; stay with a lit burner or turn the gas off.

g7c2a.title: Check-in 2A · Particles and changes of state

qs.s: Which is the school definition of matter?
o: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.
Matter is anything you can see and touch.
Matter is anything that is a solid or a liquid.
Matter is anything that gives off energy.
qs.f: Learn box, page 36: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.

qs.s: Which of these is NOT matter?
qs.f: Page 36: light, sound and heat are forms of energy. They have no mass and take up no space.

qs.s: The particle model: 1. All matter is made up of tiny [a]. 2. The particles of matter are always [b]. 3. The particles have [c] between them. 4. Adding thermal energy to matter makes the particles move [d].
qs.f: The four ideas of the particle model, Learn box, page 37.

qs.s: Match each state to its particles.
p: close together, regular pattern, vibrate in fixed positions
close together, random, slide over each other
far apart, random, move fast in all directions
x: far apart, regular pattern, do not move
qs.f: The particle pictures and table, page 38.

qs.s: Which state of matter can be squashed (compressed)?
qs.f: Pages 38 to 39: only gases can be compressed. Their particles have space to move into.

qs.s: A metal lid expands when it is heated. What happens to its particles?
o: They vibrate more and move further apart.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 39: the particles stay the same size; they vibrate more and move further apart.

qs.s: Liquids and gases can both flow. What are they called together?
qs.f: Page 38: liquids and gases can both flow, so together they are called fluids.

qs.s: Match each change to its name.
qs.f: The phase-change diagram and Learn boxes, pages 41 to 42.

qs.s: Which changes give out (release) energy?
qs.f: Exam eye, page 43: freezing, condensation and deposition give out energy.

qs.s: Boiling occurs [a] the liquid, but only at the [b]. Evaporation takes place at the [c] of the liquid only. Evaporation occurs over a [d].
qs.f: Learn box, page 42, and Worked example 2.1, page 43.

qs.s: What is the white cloud above a boiling kettle?
qs.f: Common mistake, page 42: water vapour is invisible; the white cloud is tiny droplets of liquid water.

qs.s: On a winter morning, water vapour touches a car window colder than 0 °C and changes straight into ice crystals. What is this change called?
qs.f: Science in South Africa, page 42: frost forms by deposition.

qs.s: Which state has a fixed volume but takes the shape of the bottom of its container?
qs.f: Table, page 38: a liquid has a fixed volume and takes the shape of the bottom of its container.

qs.s: At which temperature does water melt and freeze?
qs.f: Page 42: water melts and freezes at 0 °C.

g7c2b.title: Check-in 2B · Melting points, diffusion and changes

qs.s: Ethanol melts at −114 °C and boils at 78 °C. What is its state at 25 °C?
qs.f: 25 °C is between the melting point and the boiling point, so liquid (Now you, page 51).

qs.s: Substance X melts at −95 °C and boils at 56 °C. What is its state at −100 °C?
qs.f: −100 °C is colder than −95 °C: below the melting point, so solid (Worked example 2.2, page 51).

qs.s: Nitrogen melts at −210 °C and boils at −196 °C. What is its state at −200 °C?
qs.f: −200 °C is between −210 °C and −196 °C, so liquid. Draw a number line (page 50).

qs.s: Oxygen melts at −218 °C and boils at −183 °C. What is its state at 20 °C?
qs.f: 20 °C is above the boiling point, so gas (table, page 50).

qs.s: A substance melts at 80 °C. What is its freezing point in °C? Type the number only.
qs.f: A substance freezes at the same temperature as it melts (page 42).

qs.s: A substance has a melting point of −25 °C and a boiling point of 46 °C. What state is it in at 53 °C?
qs.f: 53 °C is above the boiling point, so gas (page 50, steps 2 to 4).

qs.s: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a [a] concentration to a [b] concentration.
qs.f: Learn box, page 57.

qs.s: In which state is diffusion fastest?
o: it is the same in all three
qs.f: Page 57: gas particles move fast and are far apart, so diffusion is fastest in gases.

qs.s: A drop of food colouring spreads faster through hot water than through cold water. Why?
o: The particles have more energy and move faster.
qs.f: Page 57, Warmer: faster. At a higher temperature the particles move faster, so they diffuse faster.

qs.s: A bottle of perfume is opened in a closed room with no draught. Soon the smell reaches the far corner. Why?
o: The perfume particles move on their own and spread out by diffusion.
A draught must be blowing the smell.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 57: even with no draught the particles spread out by diffusion.

qs.s: Which change is a chemical change?
qs.f: Page 59: burning makes new substances. Melting, dissolving and boiling are physical changes.

qs.s: Sugar dissolves in water. Which statement is correct?
o: It is a physical change: no new substance forms.
It is a chemical change, because the sugar disappears.
It is a chemical change, because the water tastes sweet.
It is not a change at all.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 60: dissolving is a physical change; evaporate the water to get the sugar back.

qs.s: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. The reactants are magnesium and [a]. The products are [b] and hydrogen.
qs.f: Page 59: reactants go before the arrow, products after it. Quick check 2.6, page 61.

qs.s: Which is a sign that a chemical reaction has taken place?
qs.f: Signs to look for, page 59: a gas fizzes off, a colour change, a precipitate, it gets hot or cold, light.

qs.s: Physical or chemical change?
qs.f: Pages 59 to 60: a chemical change makes a new substance; a physical change does not.

qs.s: Atoms are the [a] of matter. The atom is the smallest unit of matter that can take part in an ordinary [b].
qs.f: Learn box, page 69.

qs.s: Match each particle to where it is found and its charge.
p: in the energy shells, negative charge
x: in the energy shells, positive charge
qs.f: Learn box, page 70.

qs.s: What is the relative mass of an electron?
qs.f: Table, page 71: an electron is about 1 840 times lighter than a proton.

qs.s: Which two particles are called nucleons?
qs.f: Learn box, page 70: protons + neutrons = nucleons, because they are found in the nucleus.

qs.s: Why is an atom electrically neutral?
o: It has the same number of protons and electrons.
It has the same number of protons and neutrons.
qs.f: Learn box and Common mistake, pages 72 to 73.

qs.s: An atom has 12 protons in the nucleus. To be neutral it must also have:
qs.f: Quick check 3.3, page 73: same number of protons and electrons.

qs.s: Where is most of the mass of an atom?
qs.f: Page 71: the electrons are so light that almost all the mass is in the nucleus.

qs.s: A magnesium tile shows the numbers 12 and 24. Which is which?
o: 12 is the atomic number; 24 is the mass number.
24 is the atomic number; 12 is the mass number.
12 is the number of neutrons; 24 is the number of electrons.
qs.f: Page 74: the smaller number is the atomic number; the bigger number is the mass number.

qs.s: What is the atomic number?
o: The number of protons found in the nucleus of an atom.
The number of neutrons in the nucleus.
The total number of protons and neutrons.
qs.f: Learn box, page 73.

qs.s: What is the mass number (nucleon number)?
o: The total number of neutrons and protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The number of protons in the nucleus.
The number of neutrons in the nucleus.
The total number of particles in the atom.
qs.f: Learn box, page 73.

qs.s: Sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons are in a sodium atom? Type the number only.
qs.f: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12 (Exam eye, page 76).

qs.s: Fluorine has atomic number 9 and mass number 19. How many neutrons are in a fluorine atom? Type the number only.
qs.f: Neutrons = 19 − 9 = 10 (PEN rules, page 75).

qs.s: On the Periodic Table chlorine has atomic number 17 and relative atomic mass 35.5. How many neutrons are in the commonest chlorine atom? Type the number only.
qs.f: Use the mass number 35: neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18 (Worked example 3.4, page 77).

qs.s: Potassium has atomic number 19 and mass number 39. How many electrons are in a neutral potassium atom? Type the number only.
qs.f: Electrons = atomic number in a neutral atom (PEN rules, page 75).

qs.s: An aluminium atom has mass number 27 and atomic number 13. How many neutrons does it have? Type the number only.
qs.f: Neutrons = 27 − 13 = 14 (Now you, page 75; PEN rules, page 75).

qs.s: Where are the electrons in an atom?
o: in energy shells around the nucleus
qs.f: Page 86: electrons move around the nucleus in fixed paths called energy shells.

qs.s: Which shell has the lowest energy?
o: the smallest shell, closest to the nucleus
all shells have the same energy
qs.f: Page 86: the smallest shell, closest to the nucleus, has the lowest energy. Electrons fill it first.

qs.s: The 2-8-8 rule: the 1st energy level holds a maximum of [a] electrons, the 2nd a maximum of [b] and the 3rd a maximum of [c].
qs.f: Learn box, page 87.

qs.s: What is the electron arrangement of sodium (11 electrons)?
qs.f: 2 + 8 + 1 = 11. Table, page 88.

qs.s: What is the electron arrangement of potassium (19 electrons)?
qs.f: Common mistake, page 88: the 3rd shell takes only 8, so the 19th electron starts the 4th shell.

qs.s: Which electron arrangement shows an atom with three valence electrons?
qs.f: Valence electrons are in the outermost shell (page 91): 2,8,3 has 3.

qs.s: What is the electron arrangement of nitrogen (7 electrons)?
qs.f: Fill the 1st shell with 2, then the 2nd with the last 5 (page 88).

qs.s: Aluminium has 13 electrons. 1st shell: [a]. 2nd shell: [b]. 3rd shell: [c]. Electron arrangement: [d].
qs.f: Worked example 3.5, page 89.

qs.s: What are valence electrons?
o: Electrons that are found on the outermost energy level.
All the electrons in an atom.
qs.f: Learn box, page 91.

qs.s: Magnesium is 2,8,2. It has [a] shells, so it is in Period [b]. It has [c] valence electrons, so it is in Group [d].
qs.f: Page 92: shells = period; valence electrons = group (Groups 1 to 7).

qs.s: An atom has the electron arrangement 2,8,7. Which statement is correct?
qs.f: Worked example 3.7, page 92: 3 shells, 7 valence electrons, 17 electrons = chlorine.

qs.s: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
o: They have a full outer shell.
qs.f: Exam eye, page 92: a full outer shell does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

qs.s: Helium is in Group 8. Which statement is correct?
o: It has 2 electrons, which fill its one shell.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 92: helium is in Group 8 because its outer shell is full.

qs.s: An atom has the arrangement 2,8,6. Which element is it?
qs.f: 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 electrons: sulfur. 6 outer electrons: a non-metal (page 93).

qs.s: A Bohr diagram has two shells and 4 electrons in the outer shell. Which statement is correct?
o: 2 + 4 = 6 electrons: carbon, in Period 2 and Group 4.
qs.f: Who is right?, page 94.

g7c4a.title: Check-in 4A · Mendeleev and reading the Periodic Table

qs.s: Who first proposed the Periodic Table?
qs.f: Page 106: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements in a table (Quick check 4.1, page 107).

qs.s: Where did Mendeleev put elements that behave alike?
o: At opposite ends of the table
qs.f: Page 106: he put elements that behave alike in the same column.

qs.s: Complete the definition. The Periodic Table: The elements are arranged in [a] order of their [b].
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 106. Learn it word for word.

qs.s: How did Mendeleev first put his element cards in order?
o: in alphabetical order of their names
in order of their atomic number
in order of when they were found
in order of the mass of their atoms
qs.f: Page 106: Mendeleev arranged the cards in order of the mass of their atoms. Today we use atomic number.

qs.s: Mendeleev left gaps in his table. What did he say the gaps were for?
o: elements that were too reactive to study
elements that did not fit any column
elements with the same mass as a neighbour
qs.f: Page 106: the gaps were for elements nobody had found yet, and he predicted their properties.

qs.s: What convinced other scientists that Mendeleev's table was right?
o: He found all the missing elements himself.
Gallium and germanium were found and fitted his predictions.
He put the elements in order of atomic number.
qs.f: Page 106: gallium and germanium fitted his predictions almost exactly. That convinced other scientists.

qs.s: A tile on the school's Periodic Table gives four facts, top to bottom. Match each line to its fact.
qs.f: Page 107: atomic number, atomic symbol, name and relative atomic mass, top to bottom.

qs.s: A tile shows two numbers. How do you know which one is the atomic number?
o: The atomic number is always the bigger number.
The atomic number is always the smaller number.
The atomic number is always the bottom number.
The two numbers are always the same.
qs.f: Page 107: the smaller number is always the atomic number (proton number). The bigger one is the relative atomic mass.

qs.s: For which element are the atomic number and the relative atomic mass both 1?
qs.f: Page 107: hydrogen is the only element where both are 1.

qs.s: The chlorine tile shows 35.5. Which mass number do you use for its commonest atom?
qs.f: Page 107: chlorine (35.5) is the one to watch; its commonest atom has mass number 35.

qs.s: A question asks for the mass number of arsenic from the Periodic Table. What do you give?
qs.f: Exam eye, page 109: give the relative atomic mass as a whole number (arsenic: 75).

qs.s: Why does hydrogen sit on its own at the top of the exam table?
o: It is a non-metal gas, not like the Group 1 metals.
It is the heaviest element on the table.
It is a noble gas with a full outer shell.
It has no electrons, only one proton.
qs.f: Where is hydrogen?, page 107: it is not like the Group 1 metals; it is a non-metal gas.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many neutrons are in an atom of bromine? Type the number only.
qs.f: Bromine: 80 − 35 = 45 neutrons (Worked example 4.1, page 109).

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many neutrons are in an atom of cobalt? Type the number only.
qs.f: Cobalt: atomic number 27, relative atomic mass 59, so 59 − 27 = 32 (Now you, page 109).

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many neutrons are in an atom of phosphorus? Type the number only.
qs.f: Phosphorus: 31 − 15 = 16 (Quick check 4.2, page 109).

qs.s: Complete the definition. The [a] of the periodic table are called groups and the [b] are called periods.
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 110. Learn it word for word.

qs.s: Which statement about a group is correct?
o: A group is a single tile on the table.
A group is the block of transition metals.
qs.f: Page 110: Group 2 is a column (vertical); Period 3 is a row (horizontal).

qs.s: Name the element in Group 7, Period 4.
qs.f: Worked example 4.2, page 110: go down the Group VII column to the Period 4 row: bromine.

qs.s: Name the element in Group 2, Period 6.
qs.f: Worked example 4.2, page 110: go down the Group II column to the Period 6 row: barium.

qs.s: Match each address on the Periodic Table to its element.
qs.f: Find the column, then go down to the row (pages 110 to 111).

qs.s: Name the element in Group 6, Period 2.
qs.f: Now you, page 111: Group 6, Period 2 is oxygen.

qs.s: Name the element in Group 8 (VIII), Period 4.
qs.f: Now you, page 111: Group 8 is the noble gases, so Period 4 gives krypton. Iron has no Grade 7 group number (page 110).

qs.s: Magnesium is in Group [a] and Period [b].
qs.f: Page 110: magnesium (outlined) is in both Group 2 and Period 3.

qs.s: Argon is in Group [a] and Period [b].
qs.f: Quick check 4.3, page 111: argon is a noble gas (Group 8) in Period 3.

qs.s: How do you count the periods?
o: From the bottom: the actinoid row is Period 1.
From the left: Group 1 is Period 1.
From the top, with the lithium row as Period 1.
From the top: hydrogen and helium are Period 1.
qs.f: Page 110: count periods from the top. Hydrogen and helium are Period 1.

qs.s: Caesium starts a row of the Periodic Table. Which period is it? Type the number only.
qs.f: Page 110: Period 6 is the row that starts with caesium.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. Iodine is in which group? Use the book's Group 1 to Group 7 numbering. Type the number only.
qs.f: Iodine is in the Group VII column, below bromine (page 110).

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. Silicon is in which period? Type the number only.
qs.f: Silicon is in the third row, with sodium to argon (page 110).

qs.s: The exam table prints a Roman numeral for the noble gas group. Which one?
qs.f: Page 110: the exam table prints VIII. This book calls it Group 8.

qs.s: Which group number do the transition metals have in Grade 7?
o: They have no Grade 7 group number.
qs.f: Page 110: the transition metals in the middle have no Grade 7 group number.

qs.s: The elements that lie to the left of the zigzag line on the Periodic Table are…
qs.f: Page 111: metals to the left and below the zigzag line, non-metals to the right (Quick check 4.4, page 112).

qs.s: Complete the definition. Non-metals: [a] (as solids). Do not [b] electricity.
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 112. Learn it word for word.

qs.s: Which statement describes metalloids?
o: They are all gases at room temperature.
They are the most reactive metals.
They share properties with both metals and non-metals.
Their atoms have a full outer shell.
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 112: metalloids share properties with both metals and non-metals.

qs.s: Which element is a metalloid?
qs.f: Page 112: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium are metalloids, on the zigzag line.

qs.s: Choose the kind of element. Shiny when polished: [a]. Dull: [b]. Bend instead of breaking: [c]. Snap or crumble as solids: [d]. Semiconductor in computer chips: [e].
qs.f: Metals, non-metals and metalloids, page 112.

qs.s: Hydrogen sits above Group 1 on many tables. What kind of element is hydrogen?
o: a metalloid on the zigzag line
qs.f: Common mistake, page 112: hydrogen is a non-metal, a colourless gas.

qs.s: Which changes occur from left to right across a period?
o: Atomic number increases; metallic character decreases.
Atomic number decreases; metallic character increases.
Atomic number increases; metallic character increases.
Atomic number stays the same; metallic character decreases.
qs.f: Exam eye, page 112: across a period the atomic number increases and the metallic character decreases.

qs.s: Match each family to where it is on the Periodic Table.
qs.f: The group families, page 113.

qs.s: "Soft, silvery coloured metals. Very reactive." Which family is this?
qs.f: Definitions to learn, page 113: Group 1, the alkali metals.

qs.s: Which description matches the halogens (Group 7)?
o: Unreactive. All are gases at room temperature.
Soft, silvery coloured metals. Very reactive.
qs.f: Definitions to learn, page 113: halogens, most are poisonous; fairly reactive.

qs.s: Which three properties describe most transition metals?
o: very reactive, soft and stored under oil
unreactive gases with a full outer shell
qs.f: Definitions to learn, page 113: most are good conductors of electricity; malleable; ductile.

qs.s: Reactivity [a] down Group 1, and reactivity [b] down Group 7.
qs.f: Page 114: reactivity increases down Group 1. Page 115: reactivity decreases down Group 7.

qs.s: Francium is below caesium in Group 1. What would you expect if it were dropped into water?
o: Nothing much: it is so heavy it would just sink.
The same as lithium, because they are in one group.
No reaction, because francium is a non-metal.
An even more violent reaction than caesium.
qs.f: Who is right?, page 114: reactivity increases down Group 1, so francium would react even more violently.

qs.s: Which element is the most reactive non-metal?
qs.f: Page 115: fluorine is the most reactive non-metal; reactivity decreases down Group 7.

qs.s: Match each element to its use.
p: cleans the gases in car exhausts
x: burns with a dazzling white flame
qs.f: Page 115: Groups 7 and 8, and Science in South Africa.

g7c4d.title: Check-in 4D · Why elements in a group react alike

qs.s: Complete the definition. Each atom in the same group has the same number of electrons in its [a] (valence electrons). This is why elements in the same group usually have similar [b] properties.
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 115. Learn it word for word.

qs.s: Each atom in the same period has the same number of…
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 115: each atom in the same period has the same number of electron shells.

qs.s: For Groups 1 to 7, the group number tells you the number of…
qs.f: Period 3 table, page 116: Group 1 has 1 valence electron, Group 2 has 2, and so on.

qs.s: Atom A is 2,7. Atom B is 2,8,7. Atom C is 2,8,1. Which two elements have similar chemical properties?
qs.f: Worked example 4.3, page 116: A and B both have 7 valence electrons (both in Group 7).

qs.s: Lithium (2,1), sodium (2,8,1) and potassium (2,8,8,1) react with water in a similar way. Why?
o: Each has the same number of shells.
Each has the same number of protons.
Each has a full outer shell.
qs.f: Definition to learn, page 115: same group, same number of valence electrons, similar chemical properties.

qs.s: Which answer earns the mark? Why are the noble gases unreactive?
o: Their atoms have a complete (full) outer shell.
qs.f: Page 116: their atoms have a complete (full) outer shell. "They are stable" on its own gets no mark.

qs.s: Which pair of elements have similar chemical properties?
qs.f: Page 115: fluorine and chlorine are both in Group 7, so they have the same number of valence electrons.

qs.s: Which element reacts most like sodium?
qs.f: Potassium is in Group 1 with sodium: one valence electron each (pages 114 to 116).

qs.s: What is the electron arrangement of the element in Group 2, Period 3?
qs.f: Period 3 table, page 116: magnesium, 2,8,2 (2 valence electrons, 3 shells).

qs.s: An atom has the electron arrangement 2,8,8. Which statement is correct?
o: It is in Group 2 and reacts like magnesium.
It is in Period 8 and it is a metal.
It is in Group 8 and is very reactive.
It is in Group 8 and is unreactive: full outer shell.
qs.f: Period 3 table, page 116: argon, 2,8,8, has 8 valence electrons (full), a noble gas.

qs.s: In Period 3, silicon is 2,8,[a] and it is a [b]. Argon is 2,8,[c] and it is a [d].
qs.f: Period 3 table, page 116.

qs.s: Match each electron arrangement to its group.
qs.f: Period 3 table, page 116: the number of valence electrons gives the group.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many valence electrons does a sulfur atom have? Type the number only.
qs.f: Sulfur is in Group 6, Period 3: 2,8,6, so 6 valence electrons (page 116).

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many electron shells does a chlorine atom have? Type the number only.
qs.f: Chlorine is in Period 3, so it has 3 shells: 2,8,7 (pages 115 to 116).

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. Which element has the symbol Ag?
qs.f: Periodic Table Worksheet, page 117: 47, Ag, silver, 108.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. What is the atomic number of antimony? Type the number only.
qs.f: Periodic Table Worksheet, page 117: 51, Sb, antimony, 122.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. Which element has atomic number 76?
qs.f: Periodic Table Worksheet, page 117: 76, Os, osmium, 190.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. What is the symbol for mercury?
qs.f: Periodic Table Worksheet, page 117: 80, Hg, mercury, 201.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. Which element has the symbol Mn?
qs.f: Periodic Table Worksheet, page 117: 25, Mn, manganese, 55. Magnesium is Mg.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. What is the relative atomic mass of zinc? Type the whole number.
qs.f: Periodic Table Worksheet, page 117: 30, Zn, zinc, 65.

qs.s: Match each symbol to its element.
qs.f: The First Forty Elements crossword, page 121. Silicon is Si.

qs.s: An atom has 7 protons and 7 neutrons. Which element is it?
qs.f: Periodic Table Practice, page 118: 7 protons means atomic number 7, nitrogen.

qs.s: An atom has 8 protons and 8 neutrons. It has [a] electron shells and [b] electrons in its outer shell. The element is [c].
qs.f: Periodic Table Practice, page 118: 8 electrons, 2,6, oxygen.

qs.s: An atom has 10 protons and 10 neutrons. How many electrons are in its outer shell? Type the number only.
qs.f: Periodic Table Practice, page 118: neon, 10 electrons, 2,8, so 8 in the outer shell.

qs.s: What is the electron configuration of aluminium?
qs.f: Page 119, atom W: aluminium, 13 electrons, 2,8,3.

qs.s: An atom has the electron configuration 2,8,4. Which element is it?
qs.f: Page 119, atom Y: 2 + 8 + 4 = 14 electrons, silicon.

qs.s: Chlorine has 17 electrons. Its electron configuration is [a]. It is in Group [b] and Period [c].
qs.f: Page 119, atom X: chlorine, 2,8,7. Group 7, Period 3 (page 116).

qs.s: Which element is the transition metal with atomic number 22?
qs.f: Crossword, page 124 (8 across): titanium.

qs.s: Number 13 on the Periodic Table is [a]. The element with the symbol K is [b].
qs.f: Crossword, page 124 (2 down and 7 across).

qs.s: What are the horizontal rows in the Periodic Table called?
qs.f: Practice 1, page 124: the rows are called periods (definition, page 110).

qs.s: Which element has two electrons in its outer shell and three electron shells?
qs.f: Practice 2, page 124: 2,8,2 is magnesium, Group 2, Period 3.

qs.s: Which statements describe the elements in Group 8 (VIII)? 1 Their atoms have full outer electron shells. 2 They are unreactive metals. 3 They are monatomic gases (single atoms). 4 They are diatomic gases.
qs.f: Practice 3, page 124: full outer shells, and single-atom gases. They are not metals.

qs.s: Which statements describe changes from left to right across a period? 1 The atomic number increases. 2 The metallic character decreases. 3 The elements change from gases to solids.
qs.f: Practice 4, page 125: the atomic number increases and the metallic character decreases (Exam eye, page 112).

qs.s: State the name of the element. Group 1, Period 5: [a]. Group 6, Period 3: [b]. Group 7, Period 5: [c].
qs.f: Practice 5, page 125: rubidium, sulfur and iodine.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many neutrons are in an atom of iron? Type the number only.
qs.f: Practice 6, page 125: iron, 56 − 26 = 30.

qs.s: Use the Periodic Table. How many neutrons are in an atom of potassium? Type the number only.
qs.f: Practice 6, page 125: potassium, 39 − 19 = 20.

qs.s: Four Group 1 metals are added to cold water. Which reaction shows the least reactive metal?
o: It bursts into a lilac flame.
It explodes as soon as it touches the water.
It melts into a ball and whizzes across.
qs.f: Practice 9, page 126: fizzes steadily and floats is lithium, the least reactive (page 114).

qs.s: Which statement is true?
o: The elements in Group 7 are known as the noble gases.
All Group 1 elements are gases at room temperature.
The reactivity of the alkali metals decreases down the group.
qs.f: Practice 10, page 127: Group 7 is the halogens, Group 1 elements are solids, and alkali metal reactivity increases down the group.

qs.s: Astatine is below iodine in Group 7. Which prediction is correct?
o: More reactive: reactivity increases down every group.
Just as reactive: same group, same reactivity.
Less reactive: halogens get less reactive down Group 7.
Unreactive: its atoms have a full outer shell.
qs.f: Practice 14, page 128: the halogens become less reactive down Group 7 (page 113).

qs.s: Element X has atomic number 18. Its electron arrangement is [a]. It is in Group [b] and Period [c].
qs.f: Question 4 (a)(iii) and (iv), page 128: 2,8,8, Group 8, Period 3.

qs.s: Elements P and Q are both alkali metals. Q is lower down the group. Which reacts more violently with water?
o: P, because reactivity decreases down Group 1.
They react the same, because they share a group.
Q, because reactivity increases down Group 1.
Neither, because alkali metals do not react with water.
qs.f: Question 4 (a)(vii), page 129: Q, because reactivity increases down Group 1.

qs.s: Element T is in Group 6. How many valence electrons does an atom of T have? Type the number only.
qs.f: Question 4 (b), page 129: the group number gives the valence electrons, so 6.

qs.s: Who first proposed the Periodic Table, and how are the elements arranged in the modern table?
o: Mendeleev; in order of increasing atomic mass
Mendeleev; in order of increasing atomic number
Dalton; in order of increasing atomic number
Rutherford; in order of increasing atomic mass
qs.f: Question 4 (c), page 129: Dmitri Mendeleev; in order of increasing atomic number.

qs.s: Match each idea to what it tells you.
qs.f: The Periodic Table on a page, page 130.

qs.s: Match each word to its definition.
p: A substance composed of a single type of atom.
A substance in which two or more different elements are chemically bonded together.
Two or more substances that are mixed together but are not chemically bonded.
x: A substance in which all the atoms are separate from each other.
qs.f: Learn these word for word: element page 132, compound page 134, mixture page 136.

qs.s: What is a molecule?
o: Any substance made of only one type of atom.
Two or more substances mixed but not bonded.
A group of two or more atoms that are chemically bonded together.
The small number written after a symbol in a formula.
qs.f: Page 132: a group of two or more atoms that are chemically bonded (joined) together is called a molecule.

qs.s: In a particle picture, two atoms are drawn touching. What does this show?
o: They are bonded together into one particle.
They are always atoms of two different elements.
They are mixed together but not bonded.
qs.f: How to read a particle picture, page 133: atoms that touch are bonded together into one particle.

qs.s: A pupil writes CO when she means the element cobalt. What does CO really stand for?
o: The element cobalt, written in capitals.
A compound made of carbon and oxygen.
A mixture of carbon atoms and oxygen atoms.
qs.f: Page 133: write the second letter small. Co is cobalt; CO is a compound of carbon (C) and oxygen (O).

qs.s: Some symbols come from Latin names. The symbol for sodium is [a]. The symbol for iron is [b]. The symbol for gold is [c].
qs.f: Symbol table, page 133: sodium Na (natrium), iron Fe (ferrum), gold Au (aurum).

qs.s: How many atoms are there in one particle of CH₄ (methane)? Type the number only.
qs.f: Page 134: no number means one atom. CH₄ is 1 C + 4 H = 5 atoms (page 135).

qs.s: Copper chloride has the formula CuCl₂. It contains [a] elements. One unit of CuCl₂ has [b] atoms. Copper chloride is [c].
qs.f: Worked example 5.1, page 135: Cu and Cl are 2 elements; 1 + 2 = 3 atoms; two different elements bonded, so a compound.

qs.s: Which statement about oxygen, O₂, is correct?
o: O₂ is a compound because it has two atoms.
O₂ is a mixture because it has two atoms.
O₂ is a compound because its atoms are bonded.
O₂ is an element because both atoms are oxygen.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 135: both atoms are oxygen, so O₂ is an element. A compound needs two or more different elements.

qs.s: Which one of these is NOT a compound?
qs.f: Quick check 5.2, page 136: O₂ is made of one type of atom only, so it is an element.

qs.s: How can a compound be split up again?
o: It can never be split up.
qs.f: Page 134: a compound can only be split up again by a chemical reaction.

qs.s: Which statement about a mixture is true?
o: Each substance keeps its own properties.
The substances are chemically bonded together.
The amounts of each substance can never change.
It can only be separated by a chemical reaction.
qs.f: Page 136: in a mixture each substance keeps its own properties, and the amounts can change.

qs.s: Classify each substance. Neon is [a]. Sodium chloride, NaCl, is [b]. Sugar water is [c]. Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is [d].
qs.f: Table on page 136: neon is an element; NaCl and CO₂ are compounds; sugar water is a mixture.

qs.s: Pure gold is 24 carat. Jewellery gold is 18 carat: it is 75 % gold, with some copper or silver added to make it harder. How do we classify 18-carat gold?
o: An element, because it is mostly gold.
A compound of gold and copper.
qs.f: Science in South Africa, page 133: 18-carat gold is 75 % gold, a mixture of elements.

qs.s: A box contains only separate single atoms of two different kinds. Classify it.
qs.f: Quick check 5.4, page 139: two kinds of particle, and each part is an element, so it is a mixture of elements.

qs.s: A box has four O₂ molecules and four H₂O molecules, all mixed together. Zoe says: it is a compound, because water is a compound. Ravi says: it is a mixture of an element and a compound. Lerato says: it is a mixture of compounds, because both are molecules. Who is right?
qs.f: Who is right?, page 139: O₂ is an element and H₂O is a compound, and they are not bonded to each other.

g7c5b.title: Check-in 5B · Particle pictures, formulae and reactions

qs.s: In a chemical reaction equation, what are the substances before the arrow called?
qs.f: Practice 2, page 143, and page 139: reactants → products. The reactants come before the arrow.

qs.s: A reaction happens in a closed container. Why does the mass stay the same?
o: Atoms are not made or destroyed; they are only rearranged.
New atoms are made to replace the ones that are used up.
The products are always gases that stay inside.
The reactants do not change into new substances.
qs.f: Page 140: atoms are not made and not destroyed in a chemical reaction; they are only rearranged.

qs.s: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many hydrogen atoms are there in the products? Type the number only.
qs.f: Pages 139 to 140: 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms before, and 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms after.

qs.s: Which is the correct way to write the reaction of sodium with chlorine?
qs.f: Common mistake, page 140: chlorine gas is made of Cl₂ molecules, not single Cl atoms.

qs.s: During a chemical reaction, the atoms in the [a] [b] to form the [c].
qs.f: Quick check 5.5, page 141: the atoms in the reactants rearrange to form the products.

qs.s: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Is magnesium oxide an element or a compound?
o: An element, because it has only one formula.
A compound, because two different elements are bonded.
A mixture, because magnesium and oxygen are mixed.
An element, because it is made from two elements.
qs.f: Worked example 5.3, page 140: two different elements (Mg and O) are chemically bonded, so it is a compound.

qs.s: Hydrogen gas is written H₂. Hydrogen, H₂, is [a], because [b].

o: both of its atoms are hydrogen

qs.f: Page 132: H₂ has one type of atom only, so it is an element. Practice 8, page 144, asks the same about Cl₂.

qs.s: Classify each substance. Air is [a]. Water is [b]. Gold is [c]. Oxygen is [d].
qs.f: Practice 3, page 143: air is a mixture, water is a compound, gold and oxygen are elements.

qs.s: True or false? A compound can be separated into its elements by filtering.
o: True: filtering separates any two substances.
True: the elements in a compound are not bonded.
False: a compound can only be broken down by a chemical reaction.
False: a compound can never be split up at all.
qs.f: Practice 9, page 145: a compound can only be broken down by a chemical reaction. Filtering is for mixtures.

qs.s: Air contains nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water vapour. How do we classify air?
o: A compound of nitrogen and oxygen.
A mixture of elements and compounds.
qs.f: Practice 9, page 145: N₂ and O₂ are elements and CO₂ and water vapour are compounds, so air is a mixture of elements and compounds.

qs.s: Salt water and sodium chloride both contain sodium and chlorine. Why is sodium chloride a compound, but salt water a mixture?
o: Salt water contains more sodium and chlorine than sodium chloride.
In sodium chloride the elements are bonded; in salt water the salt and water are not.
Sodium chloride is a solid, and every solid substance is a compound.
In salt water the salt and the water are chemically bonded together.
qs.f: Practice 10, page 145: sodium and chlorine are chemically bonded in sodium chloride; salt and water are only mixed.

qs.s: Which substance is an element?
qs.f: Question 5(c), page 146: N₂ has one type of atom only, so it is an element.

qs.s: Match each formula to what is in one particle.
qs.f: Practice 7, page 144: the symbols tell you the elements; the small number tells you how many atoms (page 134).

qs.s: A box holds eight molecules, all mixed together. Four are made of two black atoms joined. Four are made of two white atoms joined. How many types of molecule are in the box? Type the number only.
qs.f: Worked example 5.2, page 138: black–black molecules and white–white molecules make 2 types. Count types, not molecules.

qs.s: Four boxes of particles. Box 1: all the particles are the same; each has two kinds of atom. Box 2: two kinds of particle; each has two kinds of atom. Box 3: one kind of atom only, joined in pairs. Box 4: separate single atoms of two different kinds. Which row describes the boxes?
o: 1 element · 2 mixture of elements · 3 compound · 4 mixture of compounds
1 compound · 2 mixture of compounds · 3 element · 4 mixture of elements
1 mixture of compounds · 2 compound · 3 mixture of elements · 4 element
qs.f: Practice 6, page 144: one compound; two kinds of compound; one element in pairs; two kinds of single atom.

qs.s: What do all acids produce when they dissolve in water?
qs.f: Definition, page 150: acids produce hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water (Quick check 6.1c, page 151).

qs.s: Match each laboratory acid to where it is found or used.
qs.f: Learn the four laboratory acids on page 151. Cement and garden lime contain calcium hydroxide, a base (page 152).

qs.s: True or False? "Sulfuric acid is found in the stomach." Choose the answer that would earn both marks.
o: False. Sulfuric acid is found in vinegar.
False. Hydrochloric acid is found in the stomach.
False. Nitric acid is found in the stomach.
qs.f: Exam eye, page 151: False, because hydrochloric acid is found in the stomach (sulfuric acid is in car batteries).

qs.s: Write acid or base for each description. Tastes sour: [a]. Feels soapy: [b]. Tastes bitter: [c].
qs.f: Definitions, pages 150 and 152: acids taste sour; bases feel soapy and taste bitter.

qs.s: What is an alkali?
o: An acid that can dissolve in water.
A base that does not dissolve in water.
A base that can dissolve in water.
qs.f: Definition, page 152: Alkali: bases that can dissolve in water (known as soluble bases).

qs.s: Which of these is an alkali?
qs.f: Quick check 6.2, page 153: sodium hydroxide is a soluble base. The other three are acids.

qs.s: Copper oxide is a base, but it does not dissolve in water. Which statement about copper oxide is correct?
o: It is a base but not an alkali.
qs.f: Page 152: copper oxide is a base, but it does not dissolve in water, so it is not an alkali.

qs.s: Which statement is correct?
qs.f: Page 152: every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.

qs.s: Match each of these to its acid.
qs.f: Acids in food and nature, page 151. Methanoic acid is in ant stings.

qs.s: You must find out whether a clear liquid in the laboratory is an acid. What should you do?
o: Taste a tiny drop, because acids taste sour.
Rub a little between your fingers.
Add an indicator and look at the colour.
Smell it closely from the bottle.
qs.f: Stay safe, page 151, and page 153: never taste or touch it; use an indicator, a dye that shows its answer as a colour.

qs.s: In an acid, blue litmus turns [a]. In a base, red litmus turns [b]. In pure water, blue litmus [c].
qs.f: Definition and notes, page 153: acid: blue litmus turns red; base: red litmus turns blue; neutral: neither paper changes.

qs.s: An unknown solution leaves red litmus red and blue litmus blue. What kind of solution is it?
qs.f: Indicator cloze, page 154: if red litmus stays red and blue litmus stays blue, it must be a neutral solution.

qs.s: Methyl orange is [a] in an acid. It is [b] in a neutral solution. It is [c] in an alkaline solution.
qs.f: Page 153: methyl orange turns red in acids and yellow in neutral and alkaline solutions.

qs.s: Why does methyl orange only tell you "acid or not acid"?
o: It is yellow in both neutral and alkaline solutions.
It is red in both acids and alkalis.
It turns green in every neutral solution.
It only works when it is on paper.
qs.f: Page 153: methyl orange cannot tell a neutral solution from an alkali, and it gives no pH number.

qs.s: In a class practical, soapy water turned universal indicator blue and methyl orange yellow. What is soapy water?
qs.f: Worked example 6.2, page 155: blue-green, blue or purple means a base; soapy water is a base.

g7c6b.title: Check-in 6B · Universal indicator and the pH scale

qs.s: Which is the school definition of pH?
o: A measure of how much water is in a substance.
A measure of how acidic or basic a substance is.
The colour that litmus turns in an acid.
A measure of how hot a solution is.
qs.f: Definition, page 155: pH: a measure of how acidic or basic a substance is.

qs.s: What is the pH of a neutral substance? Type the number only.
qs.f: The pH scale, page 155: a neutral substance has a pH of 7.

qs.s: Complete the rule: the stronger the acid, the ...
qs.f: The pH scale, page 155: the stronger the acid, the smaller the pH number.

qs.s: Four solutions have pH values 4, 1, 6 and 2. Which list goes from the least acidic to the most acidic?
qs.f: Worked example 6.3, page 156: least acidic = biggest pH below 7, most acidic = smallest pH, so 6 : 4 : 2 : 1.

qs.s: Solutions W, X, Y and Z have pH 2, 7, 9 and 13. Match each pH to the nature of the solution.
qs.f: Worked example 6.3, page 156: pH 2 strong acid, pH 7 neutral, pH 9 weak alkali, pH 13 strong alkali.

qs.s: Match each universal indicator colour to its pH range on the book's chart.
qs.f: Universal indicator colours, page 155: 0–2 red, 3–4 orange, 5–6 yellow, 7 green, 8–9 blue-green, 10–11 blue, 12–14 purple.

qs.s: Lerato says pH 13 is "a strong acid, because 13 is a big number". Is she right?
o: Lerato is wrong: pH 13 is a strong alkali.
Lerato is wrong: pH 13 is neutral.
Lerato is wrong: pH 13 is a weak acid.
qs.f: Page 156: above 7 is alkaline, and the bigger the number above 7, the stronger the alkali.

qs.s: Which substance is used to determine the strength of acids and bases?
qs.f: Exam eye, page 157: the exam answer is universal indicator (not litmus). Litmus only says acid or alkali (page 155).

qs.s: Which is the stronger acid?
qs.f: Quick check 6.4, page 157: pH 2, because the stronger the acid, the smaller the pH number.

qs.s: Give the universal indicator colour. Lemon juice, pH 2: [a]. Pure water, pH 7: [b]. Soapy water, pH 10: [c]. Milk, pH 6: [d].
qs.f: Now you, page 156, using the chart on page 155: lemon juice red, pure water green, soapy water blue, milk yellow.

qs.s: A substance has a pH of 3. What is it?
qs.f: Quick check 6.4, page 157: pH below 7 is acidic.

qs.s: Solution X has pH 10. Solution Y has pH 12. Which is the stronger alkali?
qs.f: The pH scale, page 155: the stronger the alkali, the higher the pH number.

qs.s: What colour is universal indicator in a solution of table salt?
qs.f: Page 156: pure water and a solution of table salt are neutral (pH 7): universal indicator is green.

qs.s: Why does universal indicator tell you more than litmus?
o: It shows how strong an acid or alkali is.
It turns the same colour in all alkalis.
qs.f: Page 155: universal indicator turns a different colour at different pH values, so it also shows how strong an acid or alkali is.

qs.s: Which of these shows the pH as a number on a screen?
qs.f: How to measure, page 156: a pH meter (pH sensor) shows the number on a screen.

qs.s: Which is the school definition of neutralisation?
o: A reaction in which an acid dissolves in water to make a salt.
A chemical reaction in which an acid and a base react to produce a salt and water.
A reaction in which a base turns red litmus blue and makes water.
A chemical reaction in which an acid and a base produce an indicator.
qs.f: Definition, page 157: a chemical reaction in which an acid and a base react to produce a salt and water.

qs.s: What causes indigestion or heartburn?
o: Too little acid in the stomach
Too much acid in the stomach
Too much alkali in the stomach
qs.f: Indigestion, page 159: too much acid causes indigestion or heartburn.

qs.s: What does neutralisation do to the pH number of an acid?
qs.f: Neutralisation and pH, page 157: neutralisation moves the pH number of an acid towards 7.

qs.s: Acid is added to an alkali, a little at a time. What happens to the pH of the alkali?
qs.f: Quick check 6.5, page 159: the pH decreases (goes down) towards 7.

qs.s: Sipho says: "Mixing an acid and a base always gives a solution with pH 7." Is he right?
o: Yes. Neutralisation always ends at pH 7.
No. Mixing them always gives pH 0.
No. pH 7 only when exactly the right amounts react.
No. An acid and a base do not react.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 158: the pH is 7 only when exactly the right amounts react; too much base makes it alkaline.

qs.s: Alkali is added to an acid a little at a time, with universal indicator. pH 1: [a]. pH 3: [b]. pH 5: [c]. pH 7: [d].
qs.f: Neutralising an acid, page 158: red (pH 1), orange (pH 3), yellow (pH 5), green (pH 7, neutral).

qs.s: Acid is added a little at a time to oven cleaner (pH 13) with universal indicator. How does the colour change until it is neutral?
qs.f: Neutralising an alkali, page 158: purple (pH 13), blue (pH 11), blue-green (pH 9), green (pH 7).

qs.s: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide. What are the products?
qs.f: Page 158: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride (table salt) + water.

qs.s: In chemistry, what does the word "salt" mean?
o: Only the table salt on your food.
qs.f: Page 158: salt in chemistry means the compound made in neutralisation, not only the table salt on your food.

qs.s: Vinegar has a pH of 3. Baking soda solution has a pH of 9. You add vinegar to the baking soda until they have exactly neutralised each other. What is the pH now? Type the number only.
qs.f: Worked example 6.4, page 158: exactly neutralised means pH 7 (neutral); universal indicator is green.

qs.s: Which gas makes the mixture fizz when baking soda reacts with an acid?
qs.f: Page 158: baking soda gives off carbon dioxide gas when it reacts with an acid.

qs.s: Ravi has indigestion after a huge, spicy meal. Which friend gives the right advice?
qs.f: Who is right?, page 160: an antacid is a base that neutralises the extra acid; fizzy drinks and lemon juice add more acid.

qs.s: How does toothpaste protect your teeth?
o: It contains acids that destroy the sugar.
It makes your mouth more acidic.
It turns the acid back into sugar.
It contains alkalis that neutralise the acid.
qs.f: Teeth, page 159: bacteria turn sugar into acid; toothpaste contains alkalis that neutralise the acid.

qs.s: Why do farmers spread lime on acidic soil?
o: Lime is an acid that makes the soil sour.
Lime is a base that neutralises the acid.
Lime makes the pH of the soil go down.
Lime is an indicator that shows the pH.
qs.f: Soil, page 159: farmers spread lime (a base) to neutralise acidic soil.

qs.s: The exam answer for stings: a bee sting is [a], so you use [b]. A wasp sting is [c], so you use [d].
qs.f: Stings, page 159: bee stings are acid, so use an alkali (baking soda); wasp stings are alkali, so use an acid (vinegar).

g7c6d.title: Check-in 6D · Antacids, graphs and exam practice

qs.s: A line graph earns 5 marks. Which of these is NOT one of the five things the marks are for?
o: a different colour for each point
qs.f: Drawing a line graph, page 160: heading, axis labels, scale, points and line.

qs.s: How should you join the points on a line graph, unless the question asks for a smooth curve?
o: One straight line through the middle of the points
Dot to dot with a ruler
qs.f: Drawing a line graph, point 5, page 160: join the points dot to dot with a ruler.

qs.s: Which is the correct label for the x-axis in the lime and soil experiment?
qs.f: Page 160: what you change goes on the x-axis, with units in brackets: "Mass of lime added (g)".

qs.s: An antacid investigation gave these results. 0 tablets: pH 2. 1 tablet: pH 3. 2 tablets: pH 4. 3 tablets: pH 6. 4 tablets: pH 7. 5 tablets: pH 8. After how many tablets does the stomach become neutral? Type the number only.
qs.f: Antacid worksheet, pages 165 to 166: neutral is pH 7, reached after 4 antacid tablets.

qs.s: An antacid investigation gave these results. 0 tablets: pH 2. 1 tablet: pH 3. 2 tablets: pH 4. 3 tablets: pH 6. 4 tablets: pH 7. 5 tablets: pH 8. What happens if too many antacids are taken?
o: The pH stays at 7, however many are taken.
The pH rises above 7 and the stomach becomes alkaline.
qs.f: Antacid worksheet, page 166: the pH rises above 7 (pH 8 after 5 tablets), so the stomach contents become alkaline.

qs.s: A farmer adds lime to soil. 0 g: pH 4.4. 10 g: pH 5.0. 20 g: pH 5.6. 30 g: pH 6.2. 40 g: pH 6.6. 50 g: pH 7.0. What mass of lime made the soil neutral?
qs.f: Worked example 6.5 and Now you, pages 161 to 162: the soil reaches pH 7.0 (neutral) with 50 g of lime.

qs.s: A farmer adds lime to soil. 0 g: pH 4.4. 10 g: pH 5.0. 20 g: pH 5.6. 30 g: pH 6.2. 40 g: pH 6.6. 50 g: pH 7.0. Is the soil acidic, neutral or alkaline after 30 g of lime?
qs.f: Now you, page 162: after 30 g the pH is 6.2, which is below 7, so the soil is still acidic.

qs.s: What does it mean to extrapolate a graph?
o: Join every point dot to dot with a ruler.
Extend the line beyond the last point to predict a value.
Read the value where the line meets the y-axis.
Draw one bar for each substance.
qs.f: Page 161: extending a line beyond your last point to predict is called extrapolating.

qs.s: A bar chart shows these pH values: lemon juice 2, vinegar 3, tomato juice 4, milk 6, pure water 7, baking soda 9, milk of magnesia 10, bleach 13. Which substance is the most acidic?
qs.f: Practice 7a, page 171: the shortest bar (smallest pH) is the most acidic: lemon juice, pH 2 (page 162).

qs.s: A bar chart shows these pH values: lemon juice 2, tomato juice 4, pure water 7, toothpaste 9, bleach 13. The most alkaline substance is [a]. The neutral substance is [b]. Universal indicator in toothpaste would be [c].
qs.f: Now you: read the bar chart, page 162: bleach (pH 13) is most alkaline, pure water is neutral, toothpaste (pH 9) is blue-green.

qs.s: Barry chews special gum after each meal. The gum neutralises the acid in his mouth. What type of substance neutralises an acid?
qs.f: Exam practice 1c, page 167: an alkali (a soluble base) neutralises an acid.

qs.s: Five soil samples have these pH values: A 6.0, B 7.5, C 7.0, D 4.5, E 8.0. Heather grows better in acidic soil. In which samples should heather grow well?
qs.f: Exam practice 2b, page 168: acidic means pH below 7, so A (6.0) or D (4.5).

qs.s: A facial wash has a pH of 5.5. Which describes it?
qs.f: Exam practice 3b, page 169: pH 5.5 is a little below 7, so it is slightly acidic, like healthy skin.

qs.s: Solution P has pH 5, Q has pH 1, R has pH 9 and S has pH 3. Which list goes from the least acidic to the most acidic?
qs.f: Practice 2, page 170: least acidic = biggest pH: 9, 5, 3, 1, so R, P, S, Q.

qs.s: Lerato tests solutions P, Q and R with universal indicator. P turns purple: [a]. Q turns green: [b]. R turns orange: [c]. Which one could be oven cleaner (sodium hydroxide solution)? [d]
qs.f: Question 6, page 174: P (pH 12–14) is a strong alkali and could be oven cleaner, Q (pH 7) is neutral, R (pH 3–4) is acidic.

qs.s: Which sentence is the definition of an exothermic reaction?
o: A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that releases energy into the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
A reaction that releases energy into the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
qs.f: Definitions to learn, page 178: exothermic releases energy into the surroundings, so their temperature increases.

qs.s: Which sentence is the definition of an endothermic reaction?
o: A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that releases energy into the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
A reaction that releases energy into the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
qs.f: Definitions to learn, page 178: endothermic absorbs energy from the surroundings, so their temperature decreases.

qs.s: A reaction happens in water in a beaker. In chemistry, what is the system?
o: The water the chemicals are dissolved in.
The beaker and the air around it.
qs.f: Page 177: the system is the reacting chemicals themselves; everything else is the surroundings.

qs.s: Match each word to its meaning.
p: everything else: the water, the beaker, the air and your hand
energy moves out of the system, so the surroundings get hotter
energy moves in from the surroundings, so they get colder
qs.f: Page 177: the system is the reacting chemicals; the surroundings are everything else.

qs.s: A thermometer is put into a solution where a reaction is happening. What does it measure?
o: The temperature of the reacting chemicals only.
The amount of product that forms.
qs.f: Page 177: a thermometer in the solution measures the temperature of the surroundings.

qs.s: An endothermic reaction takes place in a beaker. You hold the beaker. Which statement is right?
o: It feels hot, because the reaction absorbs heat.
It feels cold, because the reaction takes thermal energy from its surroundings, including your hand.
It feels hot, because the reaction gives out energy.
It feels cold, because the reaction gives out cold energy.
qs.f: Common mistake, page 178: an endothermic reaction feels cold. It takes thermal energy from its surroundings, including your hand.

qs.s: In an exothermic reaction the products have [a] energy than the reactants. In an endothermic reaction the products have [b] energy than the reactants.
qs.f: Definitions to learn, page 178: exothermic, products have less energy; endothermic, products have more energy than the reactants.

qs.s: Easy way to remember. EXothermic: energy [a] the reaction, and the thermometer reading goes [b]. ENdothermic: energy [c] the reaction, and the thermometer reading goes [d].
qs.f: Easy way to remember, page 178: EXothermic, energy EXits, reading up; ENdothermic, energy ENters, reading down.

qs.s: How do you calculate a temperature change?
o: the bigger reading − the smaller reading
qs.f: Page 178: temperature change = final temperature − initial temperature.

qs.s: Zinc powder is added to copper sulfate solution at 18 °C. The temperature rises to 23 °C. Calculate the temperature change in °C. Type the number only, without a + sign.
qs.f: Change = final − initial = 23 − 18 = +5 °C, so the reaction is exothermic. Now you, page 179.

qs.s: Water at 19 °C is in a cup. A pupil adds two solids and stirs. The temperature falls to 14 °C. What is the temperature change?
qs.f: Worked example 7.1, page 179: change = final − initial = 14 − 19 = −5 °C. The minus sign shows it fell.

qs.s: A temperature change is +4 °C. What does this tell you?
o: The surroundings got colder: energy was taken in. It is endothermic.
The surroundings got hotter: energy was taken in. It is endothermic.
The surroundings got colder: energy was given out. It is exothermic.
The surroundings got hotter: energy was given out. It is exothermic.
qs.f: Table on page 179: positive (+) means the surroundings got hotter, energy was given out, exothermic.

qs.s: The temperature of a solution goes from 21 °C to 16 °C. The temperature change is [a] and the reaction is [b].
qs.f: Quick check 7.2, page 180: 16 − 21 = −5 °C; the temperature fell, so it is endothermic.

qs.s: Reaction X changes the temperature by −9 °C. Reaction Y changes it by +5 °C. Which has the larger energy change?
o: Y, because a positive change is always bigger.
They have the same energy change.
X, because 9 is bigger than 5 when you ignore the sign.
You cannot compare an exothermic and an endothermic reaction.
qs.f: Exam eye, page 180: look at the size of the change and ignore the sign; −9 °C is a bigger change than +5 °C.

qs.s: Which answer for a temperature change would get full marks in the exam?
qs.f: Exam eye, page 180: always write the sign and the unit °C; "C" on its own is not accepted.

qs.s: Which of these is an exothermic reaction?
qs.f: Page 180: combustion (burning), such as a candle, gives energy out. The others take energy in.

qs.s: Which of these is an endothermic reaction?
qs.f: Page 180: in photosynthesis plants take in energy from sunlight. The others give energy out.

qs.s: Classify each one. Burning wood: [a]. Photosynthesis: [b]. An instant cold pack: [c]. Neutralisation: [d].
qs.f: Quick check 7.3, page 181, using the examples on page 180.

qs.s: Match each example to what happens.
p: burning, such as a braai fire or petrol in a car engine
plants take in energy from sunlight
calcium carbonate breaks down only while it is heated strongly
acid + base → salt + water, and the mixture warms up
x: iron powder rusting quickly when the pack is opened
qs.f: Examples to learn, page 180.

qs.s: What happens inside a hand warmer to make it hot?
o: Iron powder rusts quickly when the pack is opened.
Citric acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate.
qs.f: Hand warmers, page 180: iron powder rusting quickly when the pack is opened is exothermic.

qs.s: A paramedic squeezes an instant cold pack. A water bag inside bursts. What makes the pack go ice cold?
o: Iron powder rusts in the water.
Ammonium nitrate dissolves in the water and takes in energy.
The water freezes and gives out energy.
The water evaporates and gives out energy.
qs.f: Science in South Africa and Cold packs, pages 180 to 181: ammonium nitrate dissolves and takes energy in.

qs.s: Citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate are mixed in water. What do you observe, and what type of reaction is it?
o: It fizzes and feels warm: exothermic.
It fizzes and feels cold: exothermic.
It fizzes and feels cold: endothermic.
It fizzes and feels warm: endothermic.
qs.f: Sherbet reaction, page 180: it fizzes and feels cold, so energy is taken in: endothermic.

qs.s: Calcium carbonate only breaks down while it is heated strongly. What does this tell you?
o: It is endothermic, because energy must keep going in.
It is exothermic, because it gets very hot.
It is exothermic, because the flame gives out energy.
It is not a reaction, because it needs heating.
qs.f: Thermal decomposition, page 180: it only breaks down while heated strongly, so it takes energy in.

qs.s: Why does respiration help to keep your body warm?
o: Your cells take in energy from sunlight.
Your cells take in energy from the air.
Respiration is endothermic, so it warms you.
Your cells release energy from glucose, so it is exothermic.
qs.f: Respiration, page 180: cells release energy from glucose (you are warm!).

qs.s: Zinc is added to copper sulfate solution. What type of reaction is this?
qs.f: Metal + solution, page 180: zinc added to copper sulfate solution is exothermic, so the temperature rises.

qs.s: An acid is added to a base. Which statement is correct?
o: It is neutralisation; salt and water form and the mixture warms up.
It is neutralisation; the mixture gets colder.
It is combustion; the mixture warms up.
It is thermal decomposition; the mixture gets colder.
qs.f: Neutralisation, page 180: acid + base → salt + water, and the mixture warms up (exothermic).

qs.s: Why is melting ice not a chemical reaction, even though there is an energy change?
o: Because melting does not involve any energy.
Because no new substance forms, so it is a physical change.
Because ice is not a chemical.
qs.f: Changes that are not reactions, page 181: they are not chemical reactions, because no new substance forms.

qs.s: These physical changes involve energy. Melting: [a]. Freezing: [b]. Evaporation: [c]. Condensing: [d].
qs.f: Page 181: melting and evaporation take energy in; freezing and condensing give energy out.

qs.s: At a braai, the wood or charcoal transfers thermal energy to the meat and the air. Which reaction is this?
qs.f: Science in South Africa, page 181: the wood burns (combustion), an exothermic reaction.

qs.s: Which pair has one exothermic reaction and one endothermic reaction?
qs.f: Page 180: combustion gives energy out; photosynthesis takes energy in. The other pairs are both the same type.

qs.s: Exothermic reactions are reactions in which energy is [a] the surroundings. The temperature of the surroundings then [b]. In an exothermic reaction, the reactants have [c] energy than the products.
qs.f: Worksheet question 1, page 181: given out to, increases, more.

qs.s: Which sentence about endothermic reactions is fully correct?
o: Energy is taken in from the surroundings, the temperature decreases, and the reactants have less energy than the products.
Energy is given out to the surroundings, the temperature decreases, and the reactants have less energy than the products.
Energy is taken in from the surroundings, the temperature increases, and the reactants have more energy than the products.
Energy is taken in from the surroundings, the temperature decreases, and the reactants have more energy than the products.
qs.f: Worksheet question 1 (continued), page 182: taken in from, decreases, less.

qs.s: Which row gives one example of each type?
o: Exothermic: instant ice pack. Endothermic: hand warmers.
qs.f: Worksheet question 1, pages 181 to 182: combustion is exothermic; thermal decomposition is endothermic.

qs.s: Decide from the temperature change. Citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate in water, −5 °C: [a]. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, +30 °C: [b]. Hand warmer, +25 °C: [c]. Instant ice pack, −10 °C: [d].
qs.f: Worksheet question 2, page 182: a + change is exothermic, a − change is endothermic.

qs.s: In an endothermic reaction, which has more energy?
qs.f: Summary table, page 182: in an endothermic reaction the products have more energy than the reactants.

qs.s: During exothermic changes, [a] energy is transferred from the [b] to the [c].
qs.f: Worksheet page 183, question 1: thermal energy is transferred from the system to the surroundings.

qs.s: Which sentence describes an endothermic change?
o: Thermal energy is transferred from the system to the surroundings.
Cold energy is transferred from the system to the surroundings.
Thermal energy is transferred from the surroundings to the system.
qs.f: Worksheet page 183, question 2: during endothermic changes, thermal energy moves from the surroundings to the system.

qs.s: In a chemical reaction the substances that you react together are called [a] and the substances that form are called [b].
qs.f: Worksheet page 183, question 3: reactants react together; products form.

qs.s: Exothermic or endothermic? Absorbs energy from the surroundings: [a]. Releases energy to the surroundings: [b]. Reaction flask gets hot: [c]. Reaction flask becomes cold: [d].
qs.f: Worksheet page 184, question 4.

qs.s: In an endothermic reaction, what happens to the thermometer reading, and why?
o: It goes up, because the surroundings get warmer.
It goes down, because the surroundings get colder.
It goes up, because the reaction absorbs heat.
It stays the same, because the energy stays in the system.
qs.f: Exam practice question 2, page 184: down, because the surroundings get colder.

qs.s: Which pair are BOTH exothermic reactions?
o: A hand warmer and an instant cold pack
qs.f: Exam practice question 3, page 184: combustion, respiration, neutralisation and hand warmers are exothermic.

qs.s: Which pair are BOTH endothermic reactions?
o: Neutralisation and an instant cold pack
qs.f: Exam practice question 4, page 184: thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, cold packs and the citric acid reaction are endothermic.

qs.s: Reaction A starts at 20 °C. Its final temperature is 31 °C. Calculate the temperature change in °C. Type the number only, without a + sign.
qs.f: Exam practice question 5, page 185: 31 − 20 = +11 °C, so reaction A is exothermic.

qs.s: Reaction A: 20 °C to 31 °C. Reaction B: 22 °C to 18 °C. Reaction C: 21 °C to 25 °C. Which reaction is endothermic?
qs.f: Exam practice question 5, page 185: B is 18 − 22 = −4 °C; the temperature went down, so it is endothermic.

qs.s: Reaction A: 20 °C to 31 °C. Reaction B: 22 °C to 18 °C. Reaction C: 21 °C to 25 °C. Which reaction has the largest energy change?
qs.f: Exam practice question 5(b), page 185: A changed by 11 °C, the biggest change (compare sizes, ignore the sign).

qs.s: In the Hot or cold practical, why is the liquid put in a polystyrene cup and not a glass beaker?
o: Polystyrene does not react with the chemicals.
Polystyrene is a good insulator, so little energy is lost to or gained from the air.
Polystyrene lets the energy escape faster.
A polystyrene cup is easier to read than a beaker.
qs.f: Pages 206 and 208: the polystyrene cup is an insulator, so the temperature change is more accurate.

qs.s: In Practical 6 (Hot or cold?) you test three reactions. Which of these must you keep the same for every reaction to make the test fair?
o: The kind of solid you add
qs.f: Practical 6, question g, page 208: keep the volume of liquid, the amount of solid or the starting temperature the same.

qs.s: After you add the solid and stir, which reading do you record as the temperature after?
o: The highest (or lowest) temperature the thermometer shows
The reading just before you add the solid
The reading as soon as the solid touches the liquid
The average of the before and after readings
qs.f: Method step 4, page 206: watch the thermometer and record the highest (or lowest) temperature.

qs.s: Water starts at 21 °C. Anhydrous copper sulfate is added and the temperature rises to 27 °C. Calculate the temperature change in °C. Type the number only, without a + sign.
qs.f: Change = after − before = 27 − 21 = +6 °C, so the change is exothermic. Practical 6, page 207.

qs.s: In reaction B (citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate in water) the mixture fizzes and the thermometer reading falls. Why does it fall?
o: The reaction gives out cold energy to the water.
The gas bubbles carry the heat out of the thermometer.
The reaction releases energy into the water.
The reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so they lose energy.
qs.f: Practical 6, question d, page 208: energy comes from the surroundings (water, cup, thermometer), so their temperature falls.

qs.s: Results: A +6 °C, B −6 °C, C +8 °C. Which reactions are exothermic?
qs.f: Practical 6, question c, page 208: in A and C the temperature went up, so energy was released.

qs.s: A student dissolves ammonium nitrate in water. The thermometer falls from 25 °C to 18 °C. Which statement is correct?
o: It is exothermic because energy is released to the surroundings.
It is exothermic because the products have higher energy than the reactants.
It is endothermic because energy is released to the surroundings.
It is endothermic because the products have higher energy than the reactants.
qs.f: Practice question 1, page 186: the temperature fell, so it is endothermic and the products have more energy.

qs.s: When nitric acid reacts with calcium hydroxide, the temperature increases. Which word best describes this reaction?
qs.f: Practice question 2, page 186: neutralisation gives out energy, so it is exothermic.

qs.s: Water evaporates from the sea to form clouds. Which row describes the energy change?
qs.f: Practice question 3, page 186: evaporation takes in energy. It is a physical change, not a reaction (page 181).

qs.s: Aisha says: "Burning a candle is endothermic, because you have to light it first, which takes in energy." Why is she wrong?
o: The match only starts it; the burning candle keeps giving out energy, so it is exothermic.
She is right: anything you must light is endothermic.
Burning is a physical change, so it has no energy change.
The candle takes in energy from the air, so it is exothermic.
qs.f: Practice question 7, page 187: the match only starts the reaction; the candle keeps giving out light and warmth.

qs.s: Four solids are added to water. Changes: P +11 °C, Q −7 °C, R +8 °C, S −4 °C. Which solid gives the largest energy change?
o: Q, because its change is the most negative
S, because it fell the least
P, because 11 °C is the biggest change
qs.f: Practice question 6, page 187: P, 11 °C, is the biggest change (ignore the sign when you compare sizes).

qs.s: Sam adds a solid to a liquid and measures the temperature. Water 18 °C, add ammonium nitrate, 12 °C after: [a]. Copper sulfate solution 20 °C, add magnesium powder, 31 °C after: [b]. Dilute hydrochloric acid 19 °C, add solid sodium hydroxide, 27 °C after: [c].
qs.f: Question 7(a)(iii), page 188: the temperature fell for ammonium nitrate (−6) and rose for the other two (+11, +8).

qs.s: A hand warmer contains iron powder. When the pack is opened, it gets hot. Complete the word equation: iron + ___ → iron oxide
qs.f: Question 7(b)(ii), page 189: the iron reacts with oxygen from the air.

qs.s: An instant cold pack contains ammonium nitrate and a bag of water. The bag bursts. What happens?
o: The temperature goes up; energy is given out.
The temperature goes down; energy is taken in from the surroundings.
The temperature goes down; energy is given out.
The temperature goes up; energy is taken in.
qs.f: Question 7(b)(iii), page 189: the pack gets cold; energy is taken in from the surroundings (endothermic).

qs.s: Match each change to how it is described.
p: combustion: a reaction that gives energy out
a physical change that gives energy out
photosynthesis: a reaction that takes energy in
a physical change that takes energy in
x: thermal decomposition: a reaction that gives energy out
qs.f: Revise from this page, page 190: freezing and evaporating are physical changes (no new substance); combustion and photosynthesis are reactions.
